| Batch | Findings | Files owned | Engineer |
|---|---|---|---|
| A — rubric parsing | F-01 + F-11 (its test) | `pipeline/rubric.py`, new `tests/test_rubric.py` | 1 |
| B — batch runner | F-04/F-13 + F-12 (its test), then F-14, then F-07 | `pipeline/run_batch.py`, new `tests/test_run_batch.py` | 2 |
| C — registry config | F-02 + F-05 + F-09 | `pipeline/registry.py` | 3 |
| D — prompts | F-10 now; F-03 once answered | `prompts/grading_system.txt`, `prompts/refusal.txt` | 4 |

**Ordering:** Wave 1 runs batches A–D fully in parallel — they are file-disjoint by construction, so four engineers can work simultaneously with zero merge contact. Wave 2 is batch E plus the F-03 half of D, both gated on external answers; escalating those questions during triage means the answers arrive while Wave 1 runs, so nothing blocks.

**Reasoning for the grouping.** Batches follow file ownership, not finding numbers. Three findings each land in one small file: `pipeline/registry.py` (12 lines) is hit by F-02 (missing `aurora-1` endpoint, lines 3–7), F-05 (`DEFAULT_RUBRIC_VERSION = "rubric-v1"`, line 9), and F-09 (`DEFAULT_DATASET` pointing at the nonexistent `fixtures/eval_set_2025.jsonl`, line 11) — splitting three one-liners across engineers buys no speed and guarantees conflicts, so they bundle. `pipeline/run_batch.py` (29 lines) is hit by four items: the pagination bug (F-04/F-13, `pages()` lines 14–18), the unused `MAX_CONCURRENCY` (F-07, line 11 vs. the serial loop at lines 25–28), and the payload logging (F-14, line 27, *inside* that same loop) — one owner does them sequentially. Tests pair with the fix they cover (F-11 with F-01, F-12 with F-04/F-13) so each fix is test-first by the same person rather than coupling two engineers to one behavior. `score.py` and `test_score.py` get one owner (E) so the F-06 change and any F-08 regression test can't collide.

**Reasoning for the ordering.** Within batch B: the pagination fix first (it is the worst correctness bug — I verified a 10-row dataset currently scores **zero rows**, and 120 rows lose 20), with F-12's failing test written first; F-14's one-line log change next; F-07 last, because applying real concurrency restructures the very loop the other two touch — doing it last means one restructure instead of repeated rebases. Wave 2 last because both of its items await decisions, not because they're hard. Integration follows the single-integration-branch model: each batch branches off the integration branch's tip, is reviewed and green before folding back, and only the integration branch merges to `main` — by the trunk owner, as one change.

- **The `run_batch.py` hotspot.** Four of fourteen backlog items (F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14, plus F-12's test) target one 29-line file, `pipeline/run_batch.py`, and two of them (F-07, F-14) edit the same four-line loop (lines 25–28). Three findings each land in one small file: `pipeline/registry.py` (12 lines) is hit by F-02 (missing `aurora-1` endpoint, lines 3–7), F-05 (`DEFAULT_RUBRIC_VERSION = "rubric-v1"`, line 9), and F-09 (`DEFAULT_DATASET` pointing at the nonexistent `fixtures/eval_set_2025.jsonl`, line 11) — splitting three one-liners across engineers buys no speed and guarantees conflicts, so they bundle. `pipeline/run_batch.py` (29 lines) is hit by four items: the pagination bug (F-04/F-13, `pages()` lines 14–18), the unused `MAX_CONCURRENCY` (F-07, line 11 vs. the serial loop at lines 25–28), and the payload logging (F-14, line 27, *inside* that same loop) — one owner does them sequentially. Tests pair with the fix they cover (F-11 with F-01, F-12 with F-04/F-13) so each fix is test-first by the same person rather than coupling two engineers to one behavior. `score.py` and `test_score.py` get one owner (E) so the F-06 change and any F-08 regression test can't collide.

**Reasoning for the ordering.** Within batch B: the pagination fix first (it is the worst correctness bug — I verified a 10-row dataset currently scores **zero rows**, and 120 rows lose 20), with F-12's failing test written first; F-14's one-line log change next; F-07 last, because applying real concurrency restructures the very loop the other two touch — doing it last means one restructure instead of repeated rebases. Wave 2 last because both of its items await decisions, not because they're hard. Integration follows the single-integration-branch model: each batch branches off the integration branch's tip, is reviewed and green before folding back, and only the integration branch merges to `main` — by the trunk owner, as one change.

**2. Main risks of parallelizing, and what creates them.**

- **The `run_batch.py` hotspot.** Four of fourteen backlog items (F-04, F-07, F-13, F-14, plus F-12's test) target one 29-line file, `pipeline/run_batch.py`, and two of them (F-07, F-14) edit the same four-line loop (lines 25–28). Naive one-finding-per-engineer assignment puts three people in that file at once; textual conflicts are certain and semantic ones likely (F-07's concurrency rewrite silently reverting F-14's log fix, or vice versa).
- **The `registry.py` hotspot.** F-02, F-05, F-09 are three edits to a 12-line file, `pipeline/registry.py`. Handed to three engineers, every fold-back after the first conflicts.
- **Duplicate work.** F-04 and F-13 are the same defect — F-04 names the cause (`pages()` arithmetic, `total // PAGE_SIZE` yielding only full pages), F-13 the symptom (final partial page never scored; "filed after comparing input and output row counts"). Assigned separately, two engineers fix the same function twice and one entire batch is wasted effort plus a conflict.
- **A stale finding causing churn.** F-08 claims `score.py` raises on null/empty answers, but current `main` (`f3cac92`) already returns `{"score": 0.0, "empty": True}` (`pipeline/score.py:7-9`; I executed it to confirm). An engineer working it as written hunts for a nonexistent raise or "re-fixes" working code — and churns the same `score.py` that F-06's owner needs.
- **A shared test resource.** `tests/conftest.py:4` defaults the suite's results database to a machine-global path: `RESULTS_DB = os.environ.get("RESULTS_DB", "/var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db")`. Engineers (or agents on one machine) running tests concurrently without overriding `RESULTS_DB` collide on that file and get flaky cross-contaminated runs.
- **Behavior coupling through scores.** F-06 changes what borderline answers score (`PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS`, `pipeline/score.py:3`). Run in parallel with anything else touching `score.py`/`test_score.py`, or with new tests that assert specific 0.5/1.0 scores, it invalidates teammates' green tests mid-campaign.
- **No integration point exists yet.** `git remote -v` in `outputs-review` returns nothing — there is no origin, one local branch, one commit. Until a shared remote (or a designated worktree host) and an integration branch exist, "parallel" engineers produce divergent local-only repos that are invisible to each other and one disk failure from gone.
- **Minor: fixture contention.** F-12's boundary test needs datasets sized at an exact page multiple and multiple-plus-one (`PAGE_SIZE = 50`). If written against the shared `fixtures/eval_set.jsonl` (2 rows, also referenced by F-02's `aurora-1` check) instead of test-local data, it bloats a shared fixture and couples batches B and C.

**3. Items I would NOT hand out as written.**

- **F-06 — escalate, don't assign.** "Tighten the thresholds" specifies no target values, and any change to `PARTIAL_CREDIT_THRESHOLDS = (0.35, 0.65)` (`pipeline/score.py:3`) changes produced scores for real borderline answers — that's a scoring-policy decision, not a bug with a determinable fix. It needs the reviewer/owner to supply concrete values, ideally with a before/after re-score of a known dataset, before anyone writes code.
- **F-08 — drop; it's already fixed.** Current code at `pipeline/score.py:6-9` returns `{"score": 0.0, "empty": True}` for `None` and whitespace-only answers — verified by execution, not just by reading. Record a one-line "already fixed on `main` @ `f3cac92`" and at most convert it into a regression-test task folded into batch E.
- **F-04 + F-13 — dedupe first.** Same root cause in `pipeline/run_batch.py`'s `pages()`; assign once, to batch B, with F-12 as its test.
- **F-03 — incomplete as specified.** The fix is "point it at the rubric name," but nothing in the repository defines a named refusal rubric: `prompts/` holds only the two text files, there is no rubrics directory, and `Rubric` (`pipeline/rubric.py`) is constructed from raw text with no name concept. The engineer literally cannot complete the instruction without the reviewer supplying the rubric's actual name/location — send that question out at triage alongside F-06, and let batch D finish F-10 meanwhile.

**4. Per-engineer local setup.**

- **A workspace of their own**: a clone (or sibling git worktree) of `outputs-review` at `main` `f3cac92` — never a shared checkout. Precondition for that: the lead must first create the shared remote and an integration branch, since today the repo has no remote at all (`git remote -v` is empty), then each batch branches off the integration tip.
- **Python 3 and pytest.** The pipeline is pure stdlib (`json`, `logging`, `pathlib`, `os` are the only imports; there is no `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`), and the test suite is pytest-convention (`tests/conftest.py`); I confirmed Python 3.8.3 + pytest 5.4.3 run it on this machine.
- **Run from the repo root**, so `from pipeline.score import ...` (used by `run_batch.py` and `tests/test_score.py`) resolves — there's no installed package or packaging config; imports rely on the root being on `sys.path`.
- **A private `RESULTS_DB`**: export `RESULTS_DB=<per-engineer path>` before running tests, overriding the shared `/var/tmp/llm-scoring/results.db` default in `tests/conftest.py:4`, so parallel suites don't collide.
- **The coordination artifacts**: the deduped assignment sheet with the file-contention map (who owns `run_batch.py`, `registry.py`, `score.py`), and the shared progress/checkpoint file with resume instructions, appended to after every fold-back.
- **A green baseline**: run the existing one-test suite (`tests/test_score.py::test_full_credit`) once before starting, and note `PAGE_SIZE = 50` (`pipeline/run_batch.py:10`) when constructing F-12's boundary fixtures. Also be aware the repo has **no `.gitignore`**, so `__pycache__/` from any pytest run shows up as untracked noise (it bit my read-only inspection); adding one should be the integration branch's first commit.
sections.confidence and gaps:
- **High confidence** in the re-baseline of the code findings — F-01, F-04/F-13 (including the severity upgrade: sub-50-row datasets score nothing), and F-08's already-fixed status were verified by executing the actual module code, and F-02/F-05/F-07/F-09/F-14 are directly visible in the cited lines of `registry.py`/`run_batch.py`. High confidence in the contention map: the full file inventory is small and I read every file.
- **High confidence** in the git ground truth (single local `main`, clean, no remote) — though I can only see this machine; if the team has a hosted copy of this repo elsewhere with open PRs, that's invisible from here and would need re-checking against that remote before assigning anything.
- **Medium confidence** on F-03 and F-05's intent: I verified no named refusal rubric and no `rubric-v3` artifact exist *in this repo*, but both may exist in an external system (the sibling repos here are unrelated projects per the workspace `README.md`, and I did not audit them for shared rubric definitions). The "current rubrics are v3" claim rests on the finding plus the code comment at `registry.py:9`, not an artifact I could inspect.
- **Not verified**: I did not run the pytest suite end-to-end (avoided after the `--version` probe alone side-effected a cache file, which I removed; `git status` confirmed the tree pristine afterward), so "the existing test passes" is an inference from reading `test_score.py` against `score.py`, not an observed green run. Correct thresholds for F-06 and effort estimates per batch are inherently unverifiable from the repo.

sections.plan: The task: design a parallelization plan for clearing FINDINGS.md (F-01–F-14) in `outputs-review/` across several simultaneous engineers, without modifying anything. I set out to (1) read the campaign-planning guide I was pointed at, (2) locate the right repository in this multi-repo workspace, (3) re-baseline every finding against the actual current code rather than trusting the backlog text — checking for already-fixed items, duplicates, and underspecified behavior changes, (4) build a file-contention map to drive batch boundaries and wave ordering, (5) check git ground truth (branch tip, remotes, open PRs, stray branches, progress files), and (6) identify what each engineer needs locally, including isolated test resources.
